concepts.def: Rock containing enough of a metal compound to make extraction worthwhile.
Metals less reactive than carbon (e.g. iron) are extracted by heating with coke in a blast furnace.
Tall furnace producing iron from iron oxide using coke, limestone and hot air.
Used for very reactive metals (Al, Na) because carbon can't reduce them.
Plants absorb metal ions; burning them gives an ash high in metal compounds.
Bacteria break down low-grade ores to give leachate solutions containing metal ions.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Metals — a core area of GCSE Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Metals brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Metals.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Iron is extracted in a blast furnace using:
options: electrolysis
carbon reduction
acid reaction
distillation

mcqs.q: Why is aluminium more expensive to extract than iron?
options: aluminium is rarer
electrolysis uses lots of electricity
aluminium ore is heavy
aluminium is dense

mcqs.q: What is the relationship between two enantiomers?
options: Enantiomers are the same molecule drawn differently on paper.
They are non-superimposable mirror images that rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions but have identical chemical and physical properties otherwise.
Benzene cannot react with electrophiles at all.
Enantiomers have different boiling points and react completely differently with all reagents.
Hess's Law works because reactions can only happen in one specific direction.
Enantiomers are the same molecule drawn differently on paper.
Hess's Law works because energy always cancels out around any cycle.
Enthalpy is a state function — change depends only on initial and final states, not the route taken.

mcqs.q: Why does benzene undergo electrophilic SUBSTITUTION but alkenes undergo electrophilic ADDITION?
options: Substitution preserves benzene's stable delocalised pi system; addition would destroy aromaticity at a large energetic cost.
Enantiomers are the same molecule drawn differently on paper.
Benzene cannot react with electrophiles at all.
Benzene reacts the same way as alkenes — by addition across one of its double bonds.
